chapters.title: Chapter 5: Claiming Your TDS Credit and Refund

lessons.title: When the Deductor Gets It Wrong: Late Deposits, Wrong PAN and Missing Credits

body.text: When a TDS credit goes missing, the law is firmly on your side: tax already deducted from you cannot be demanded from you again. But the repair can only be made by the deductor, so your real job is to prove the deduction, chase the right person and escalate in the right order.

children.text: Kavita, from Lesson 1, was still missing ₹3,000 of TDS from a training company in late June. Vinod, a nurse in Kochi, found his entire year of salary TDS absent because his employer had typed one digit of his PAN wrong. Sameena, a copywriter in Bhopal, discovered that a client had deducted her TDS and simply never deposited it. Three different failures, three different fixes, and one common rule: only the deductor can correct the record.
Five Ways a Credit Goes Wrong

cells: No entry at all for a payer
Quarterly statement not filed yet, or filed with a wrong PAN
Deductor files or corrects the statement
Only part of the year shows
One quarter missing or still being processed
Deductor files the missing quarter
Entry with status U
Challan details in the statement do not match any deposit
Deductor corrects the challan details
Entry with status O
More credit claimed against a challan than was deposited
Deductor deposits the shortfall or corrects the statement
Credit in the wrong year or under the wrong income type
Statement filed for the wrong period or payment code
Deductor files a correction statement

body.text: None of these can be fixed by editing your return. Claiming a credit that is not in your statement usually produces a demand when the return is processed. The sequence that works is: prove it, chase it, escalate it, and only then file or revise.

markDefs.definition: The rule that a deductee cannot be asked to pay tax that has already been deducted from their income by the payer, even if the payer never deposited it with the government.

children.text: Section 401 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (formerly Section 205) says that where tax has been deducted at source from your income, you cannot be called upon to pay that same tax again. This is the
. The recovery has to be pursued against the deductor, not you. Tax authorities have also instructed officers not to enforce recovery from deductees in such cases.

body.text: The protection works only if you can show the tax was actually deducted. Keep payslips, invoices showing the net amount received, bank statements, TDS certificates and any email where the payer confirms the deduction. Without evidence, a missing credit simply looks like unpaid tax.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Protection
body.textWithBlank: Under Section ___ of the Income-tax Act, 2025, formerly Section 205, tax already deducted from your income cannot be demanded from you again.
body.explanation: Section 401 bars a direct demand on the deductee for tax that a deductor has already deducted. The department must recover it from the deductor, who also faces interest and penalties.

children.text: Knowing the deductor's exposure is useful leverage when you ask for a correction, because delay is far more expensive for them than for you.

body.caption: Consequences for a deductor who slips

cells: Failure to deduct
1% a month from when it was deductible until it is deducted
Section 398, formerly 201(1A)
Deducted but deposited late
1.5% a month from deduction until deposit
Section 398, formerly 201(1A)
Statement filed late
₹200 a day, capped at the TDS amount
Section 427, formerly 234E
Statement not filed, or filed with incorrect details
Penalty of ₹10,000 to ₹1,00,000
Section 461, formerly 271H
Deducted but not deposited at all
Prosecution, with rigorous imprisonment of three months to seven years plus fine
Section 476, formerly 276B
Business expense on which TDS was not deducted
30% of the expense disallowed in the deductor's own tax computation
Business income provisions

body.title: Try It: The Cost of a Seven-Month Delay
body.prompt: Sameena's client deducted ₹45,000 in June 2026 and finally deposited it in December 2026, 7 months later counting part months as full. At 1.5% a month, how much interest does the client owe on top of the tax?
body.explanation: ₹45,000 × 1.5% × 7 = ₹4,725. If the quarterly statement was also 100 days late, add a fee of ₹200 a day, which is ₹20,000 here, capped at the TDS amount. None of this comes out of Sameena's pocket, but all of it is a reason for the client to fix the problem quickly.

events.title: Ask the deductor, in writing
events.description: Email the payroll or accounts team with your PAN, the payment dates and amounts, the TDS deducted and the quarter involved. Ask for the TDS certificate and, if the credit is missing or unmatched, for a correction statement.

events.title: Follow up with a deadline
events.description: Keep everything on email so you have a record. Most problems end here, because the deductor faces interest and penalties for leaving it unfixed.

events.title: Raise a grievance on TRACES
events.description: A deductee can submit a Request for Resolution against the deductor's TAN. The request is routed to the deductor and can be tracked until it is closed.

events.title: Use the e-filing grievance channel
events.description: Lodge a grievance on the income tax portal describing the deductor, the amounts and the steps you have already taken.

events.title: Approach the TDS officer
events.description: Write to the Assessing Officer (TDS) having jurisdiction over the deductor, enclosing your evidence. That officer has the power to pursue the deductor.

events.title: Protect yourself in your own file
events.description: If a demand has already been raised on you, respond to it citing Section 401 with proof, and file a rectification request under Section 287 (formerly Section 154) if the intimation ignored a credit you were entitled to.

body.title: Quick Check: Who Fixes an Unmatched Entry?
body.question: Vinod's salary TDS shows in his statement with status U, because the employer quoted challan details that do not match any deposit. Who can correct it?
options: Vinod, by editing the entry in his AIS feedback
Vinod, by claiming the credit in his return anyway
The employer, by filing a correction statement
The bank where the tax was deposited
body.explanation: Only the deductor can file a correction statement to fix challan details, PANs, amounts or periods. AIS feedback records your objection but cannot create or repair a credit, and claiming an unmatched credit in your return usually leads to a demand.

body.title: When the wrong PAN was quoted

children.text: A wrong PAN is the most common reason an entire year of salary TDS vanishes. The tax was deposited, but against someone else's PAN or against no valid PAN at all. The employer must file a correction statement for each affected quarter with your correct PAN.

Corrections of this kind are subject to system limits on how much of a PAN can be changed in one go, so a badly mistyped PAN may need more than one attempt or a different correction route. Give your employer a clear copy of your PAN card, ask for the revised TDS certificate once the correction is processed, and check your statement again after a couple of weeks.
When the Income and the TDS Fall in Different Years

Sometimes nothing is wrong except timing: you reported income in one year and the payer deducted tax on it in a later year, so the credit arrives after the return claiming that income. For such cases there is a separate application, Form 102 (formerly Form 71), which lets the department give you credit for the earlier year. It must generally be filed within two years from the end of the year in which the tax was deducted.

body.title: Scenario: The Client That Disappeared
body.scenario: Sameena's client deducted ₹45,000 from her fees across the year but never deposited it and has now shut down. The credit never appeared in her statement. She filed her return claiming the ₹45,000, and the intimation has disallowed it, leaving a demand plus interest.
body.prompt: What are her options, and does she have to pay?
body.modelAnswer: She should not pay tax that was already deducted from her. Under Section 401 she cannot be asked to pay the same tax twice, and the department must recover it from the deductor. Practically, she should respond to the demand on the portal, disagreeing and attaching proof: invoices showing the gross fee, bank statements showing she received the amount net of ₹45,000, and any communication from the client confirming the deduction. She should file a rectification request under Section 287 so the intimation can be corrected, and raise a grievance naming the deductor and its TAN, including through TRACES. It is worth writing to the Assessing Officer (TDS) for that deductor as well, since recovery, interest under Section 398 and even prosecution under Section 476 are aimed at the defaulter. The process takes patience, but paying the tax again is not the answer, and never claim a credit you cannot evidence.

body.title: Before You Escalate
steps: Collect payslips or invoices showing the gross amount and the TDS deducted
Add bank statements showing the net amount you actually received
Save any TDS certificate you received, and note the deductor's TAN
Take a dated screenshot or download of your statement showing the credit missing or unmatched
Write to the deductor with all of this, and keep the email trail
If there is no fix within a few weeks, raise a grievance on TRACES and the e-filing portal, and write to the TDS officer

body.label: TRACES
body.description: Register as a taxpayer to view your tax credit statement and submit a Request for Resolution against a deductor whose reporting is wrong or missing.

cards.definition: Bar on direct demand. Tax already deducted from you cannot be recovered from you again. Formerly Section 205.
Interest of 1% a month for late deduction and 1.5% for late deposit, payable by the deductor. Formerly Section 201.
Late filing fee of ₹200 a day for TDS statements, capped at the TDS amount. Formerly Section 234E.
Penalty of ₹10,000 to ₹1,00,000 for not filing or for incorrect TDS statements. Formerly Section 271H.
Prosecution for failure to deposit TDS, with imprisonment of three months to seven years. Formerly Section 276B.
Rectification of a mistake apparent from the record, used when an intimation ignores a credit. Formerly Section 154.
Application for TDS credit where the income was reported in an earlier year, filed within two years. Formerly Form 71.
A grievance a deductee can raise on TRACES against a deductor over missing or wrong TDS reporting.

points: Only the deductor can repair a TDS credit, whether the problem is a missing statement, a wrong PAN, an unmatched challan or a wrong year
Section 401, formerly 205, means tax already deducted from you cannot be demanded from you again, provided you can prove the deduction
Deductors face 1% and 1.5% monthly interest, ₹200 a day fees, penalties up to ₹1,00,000 and even prosecution, which is your leverage
Escalate in order: written request to the deductor, grievance on TRACES, grievance on the e-filing portal, then the TDS officer
If an intimation has already disallowed a genuine credit, respond to the demand with evidence and file a rectification under Section 287
Where income was reported in an earlier year but TDS came later, use Form 102, formerly Form 71, within two years

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal or investment advice. Names and amounts are illustrative. Section numbers, forms, grievance routes and administrative practice reflect the position understood at the time of writing and can change. For a disputed demand or a deductor who will not cooperate, consult a qualified chartered accountant or tax advocate.
